idiom_name: blank identifier discard `_ = f()` with a justifying comment
implementation_notes: Go has no exceptions; the error is an ordinary second return value, and the mute is the blank assignment `_ = f()`. Effective Go presents the blank identifier precisely as the way to discard a value deliberately, which makes the mute visible and greppable - but Go's culture and tooling treat an unchecked error as a defect (errcheck, staticcheck, golangci-lint), so every mute needs the reason written next to it and, where a linter runs, an explicit local suppression. Where the operation can be expressed without a failure path, prefer that (os.RemoveAll, map deletion, a presence check); where only one error value is tolerable, use the narrow check idiom shown in the sketch instead of discarding the error.
pitfalls: errcheck and staticcheck report every unchecked error, so a mute without a comment (and without //nolint:errcheck where the linter runs) fails CI; disabling the linter project-wide to make the discard legal removes the guard for all the real mistakes.

The blank identifier discards the value, not the intent: `_ = f()` is textually identical whether the ignore was reasoned about or overlooked, so the comment is the only artefact carrying the justification.

Ignoring the error of a deferred Close hides the flush/write-back failure Go's Close-with-error API exists to surface - collect it in a named return (`defer func() { if err := f.Close(); err != nil { ... } }()`).
